title: Referrals and repeat work from existing clients for Construction-site clean-up
audience: Owners of construction-site clean-up businesses who want repeat site work and referrals from the principal contractors and builders they already serve.
learningOutcomes: Plan a review or referral request that is made after the client confirms the result and that the client can decline easily.
Write a next-service offer with a date, a scope and a price approach, and schedule the check-in that follows it.
Write referral reward terms, including the condition for payment, before any referral is made.

instruction.heading: Ask at the moment the client is most satisfied
instruction.body: The best time to ask for a review or referral is after the client has confirmed that the result is right, usually at sign-off or when the invoice is paid. On a construction site, that is often at the end of a stage, when the principal contractor has accepted the site housekeeping and the trades have moved on. The AMA says timing depends on the type of product, and that experience goods need more evaluation time than search goods (AMA, 10 January 2023). In one Baylor Keller Center experiment, reviews rose from 1.32 per cent of customers with no reminder to 2.16 per cent with a late reminder (1 June 2024). Ask in one sentence, name the next step you want, and make it easy to decline. Sending a review link or QR code is allowed, and Google provides one (Google Business Profile Help). Do not write or invent reviews. Asking only satisfied clients is called review gating, which Podium says Google treats as a violation (2 May 2022, a vendor source). The ACCC says incentives for reviews must be disclosed and must not depend on what the review says (15 July 2026). Google also bans discounts or goods in exchange for reviews. Do not photograph a site for a review or a showcase without the principal contractor's consent and the site rules.

instruction.heading: Offer the next service before the client leaves
instruction.body: Repeat work is one of the most dependable sources of growth for a small service business. At the end of a stage, propose the next step with a date: the clean-up for the next stage of the same project, a final clean before practical completion, or a site housekeeping contract for the next project. Put the scope, the interval and the price approach in writing, and confirm that the principal contractor agrees before you change any schedule. If the written offer goes by email, check the Spam Act first: ACMA's guidance indicates that inferred consent is narrow and does not cover a message sent just after a purchase. If a recurring contract renews automatically, a law-firm summary says renewal notices and online cancellation rules take effect on 1 July 2027 (McCullough, 3 July 2026), so set out the renewal and cancellation terms now.

instruction.heading: Check in at the interval that suits the service
instruction.body: Schedule a check-in after a period that suits the work. For a site, the natural check-in is at the end of each stage, when the principal contractor reviews progress. A suggested starting point for a longer contract is about ninety days, which is a choice to test, not a benchmark. The check asks whether the housekeeping standard still holds, whether the site rules have changed and whether there is other work to quote. Keep it short, record what the principal contractor said, and close the loop with a reply. A message that promotes any service can be commercial, even when it is framed as a reminder (Clayton Utz, 9 November 2023), so keep check-ins factual and check each one against the Spam Act. ACMA's summary (read 2026-11-04) does not say whether one-to-one messages are covered, so check that point before you send.

instruction.heading: Re-contact previous clients before their busy periods
instruction.body: Plan a short message to previous principal contractors a few weeks before a date you already know about: a project's known start of works, a stage that has been scheduled in writing, or a new project the contractor has announced publicly. Offer the slots you can actually deliver, on written terms, with a clear way to opt out. Do not use the message to pressure anyone, and do not contact a client who has asked not to hear from you. ACMA's guidance says an unsubscribe must be honoured within five working days, so record each opt-out as soon as you receive it and stop sending to that client. At the end of the period, review the response and note which timing worked. Do not contact site staff directly with offers. Route messages through the principal contractor's office or tender team.

instruction.heading: Set referral rewards in writing before anyone refers
instruction.body: A referral reward works best when the referrer knows the terms before they refer someone. Decide what you will offer, such as a credit on the next service or a small thank-you, and write down the condition for payment, which is normally that the referred business has completed a paid job. Research on referral programmes found that stating the referrer's reward in the invitation increased referrals across seven studies (Xu, Yu and Tu, 2023), so say what the reward is in the invitation. Get the referred person's consent before any referral message is sent, because the referrer's word alone may not be enough (Clayton Utz, 11 May 2017, an older source). Principal contractors often have their own rules on gifts, commissions and approved subcontractors, so check the principal contractor's contract and approval process before offering a reward. No business.gov.au or ACCC guidance on referral rewards was found, so the tax and contract effect of any reward is unconfirmed.

procedure: After each stage is signed off, make one review or referral request and record what was asked and the answer.
Write the next-service offer with a date, scope, interval and price approach, and confirm it with the principal contractor.
Schedule the check-in at the end of each stage, and send any written message using the electronic message rules.
Plan a re-contact message for each date the contractor has given you in writing, and exclude anyone who has opted out.
Write the referral reward terms and the payment condition before the first referral is made.
When a referral books, confirm the referred job is paid before applying the reward, and record the outcome.
Review at the end of each project which requests, offers and timings produced repeat work.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner completes the clean-up for the first stage of a $400,000 renovation. The site foreman says the principal contractor's project manager may recommend her on the next project. She wants to offer a credit on her next invoice if the principal contractor books her.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should she do before the principal contractor books, and what should she avoid?
workedExamples.reasoning: She writes down the reward terms before any referral happens: the credit, the condition that the principal contractor books and the job is paid, and when the credit will be applied. She asks the project manager to pass on the next project's details, and she contacts the contractor's office only if they agree. She checks the principal contractor's approval and gifts rules before offering anything. She does not promise a reward she has not written down, and she does not discuss the reward with site staff. If she is unsure of the tax or contract effect of a credit, she confirms it with an adviser. She takes on only the work her licence and insurance cover.

equipmentAndPpe: Client record with the sign-off date and the review or referral request made
Next-service offer template with scope, interval and price approach
Calendar of contractor-given dates for re-contact
No PPE is needed for client follow-up; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Asking for a review before the principal contractor has confirmed the result.
commonErrors.prevention: Ask after the stage is signed off, once the site has been accepted.

commonErrors.error: Offering a referral reward that was never written down, so the terms are disputed later.
commonErrors.prevention: Write the reward and its payment condition before any referral is made, and give the referrer a copy.

commonErrors.error: Publishing a contractor's name, logo, site photo or review without consent, or photographing a site for promotion
commonErrors.prevention: Get written consent for each thing you plan to publish, and follow the site rules before taking any photo.

commonErrors.error: Contacting a client who asked not to hear from you, or contacting site staff directly with offers.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep an opt-out list, honour each opt-out within five working days at most, and route all offers through the principal contractor's office.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Publishing a contractor's name, logo, site photo, review or project detail needs the consent of the person concerned for that use. Do not write reviews on a client's behalf or invent them. If the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) applies to your business, client contact details are personal information. Its coverage of small business is not confirmed in the research file, so check it before relying on it.

Review platforms and referral programmes can have their own rules on incentives. Google bans discounts or goods in exchange for reviews. The ACCC says incentives must be disclosed and must not depend on the review's content (15 July 2026). Principal contractors may have approval, gift and commission rules in their contracts. Check each platform's rules and each contract before offering any reward.

Check-in and re-contact messages sent by email or text can be commercial electronic messages under the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). A message that promotes any service can be commercial even when it is framed as a service reminder, and ACMA has been enforcing this area, so check each message before sending.

A referral does not extend the licence or authority of the business that accepts the work. Accept only the work your licence and insurance cover, in the state where the work is done. Licence rules differ between states, so check the rules for each state you work in. Follow the site's own safety rules and induction before any work begins. This lesson does not grant any licence.

qualityStandard: Every review or referral request is made after sign-off or payment, and it includes an easy way to decline.
Every next-service offer is written, has a date and is confirmed by the principal contractor before the schedule changes.
Every referral reward has written terms and a payment condition, and is paid only when that condition is met.
documentationEvidence: Review or referral request log with the date sent and the answer.
Next-service offers with the date, scope, interval and contractor confirmation.
Referral reward terms with the referral record and payment outcome.
summary: Ask for reviews and referrals after the stage is signed off, and make it easy to say no.
Offer the next stage or project in writing, with a date, before the site closes.
Set referral rewards and their payment conditions in writing, and check the principal contractor's rules first.

knowledgeChecks.question: When is the best time to ask a principal contractor for a review or referral?
options: Before the site opens, so the contractor feels committed
After the stage is signed off and the contractor has confirmed the result is right
Only when a trade on site has sent you a complaint

knowledgeChecks.question: A principal contractor wants to publish a review with its name and a photo of the site you cleaned. What do you need?
options: Its consent for the name and photo you plan to publish, and the site rules satisfied
Nothing, because the review is positive
Your own judgement that the photo looks professional

knowledgeChecks.question: What should a referral reward look like?
options: Paid to anyone who mentions your name on site
Decided after the referred contractor books, based on how keen the referrer seems
Decided and written in advance, with the condition for payment stated

knowledgeChecks.question: When does the lesson say to propose the next step for the client?
options: At the end of each job, with a date

Baylor Keller Center, 'Wait Just a Minute', https://kellercenter.hankamer.baylor.edu/news/story/2024/wait-just-minute-when-ask-online-reviews, 1 June 2024 (metadata says 13 May 2024). One experiment only.

AMA, article on the timing of requests for customer reviews, https://www.ama.org/2023/01/10/asking-for-customer-reviews-at-the-right-time-sooner-is-not-always-better/, 10 January 2023. Supports: timing depends on product type.
Podium, 'Review gating', https://www.podium.com/article/review-gating, 2 May 2022. Vendor source; the Google position it describes was not checked against Google's own policy.

Xu, Yu and Tu, Journal of Marketing Research 60(2), 2023, https://research.polyu.edu.hk/en/publications/i-will-get-a-reward-too-when-disclosing-the-referrer-reward-incre/. Supports: stating the referrer's reward in the invitation increased referrals across seven studies. No figures used.

Clayton Utz, 'Referrer beware', https://www.claytonutz.com/insights/2017/may/referrer-beware-proceed-with-caution-when-contemplating-refer-a-friend-promotions, 11 May 2017 (older than 2022). Supports: the referred person's consent.

Clayton Utz, 'The ACMA cranks up enforcement', https://www.claytonutz.com/insights/2023/november/the-acma-cranks-up-enforcement-do-your-factual-customer-emails-pass-the-spam-act-test, 9 November 2023. Supports: a reminder that promotes a service can be commercial.

McCullough, article on unfair trading practices laws in Australia, https://mccullough.com.au/2026/07/03/unfair-trading-practices-laws-australia-2027/, 3 July 2026. Law-firm summary. Supports: renewal and cancellation rules take effect 1 July 2027.
ACMA, 'Avoid sending spam', https://www.acma.gov.au/avoid-sending-spam, no date shown; read 2026-11-04. Supports: unsubscribe within five working days; inferred consent is narrow.

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam
officialReferences.covers: Says commercial messages cannot be sent without the recipient's permission or consent; messages must accurately identify the sender and include correct contact details; every commercial message must contain an unsubscribe option under the Spam Act 2003, which the page says sets out responsibilities under Australian law. Does not mention one-to-one messages. Publisher: ACMA.
